newsitem.title: USA: SEC chief vows to use economists more on new rules.
newsitem.headline: SEC chief vows to use economists more on new rules.

text.p: Amid growing Congressional heat, Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt this week vowed to make better use of the agency's economists when designing new regulations.

"I have already taken steps to ensure that the Commission's Office of Economic Analysis is consulted at an early stage of all regulatory initiatives," Levitt promised Phil Gramm, the Texas senator who chairs the Senate Banking Committee's securities subcommittee,in an April 9 letter.

Levitt's latest move comes as Gramm and Rep. David McIntosh, the Ohio Republican who chairs the regulatory subcommittee of the House Government Reform and Oversight Committee, are considering a plan to overturn a new SEC rule that requires companies to disclose more information about the complex financial instruments they hold.
"McIntosh is seriously considering that and he and Gramm will make a decision by the end of April," an aide to McIntosh's committee said.

The rules, which have met with wide opposition, even from within the agency, have put the SEC in the hot seat with lawmakers, particularly in light of strong criticism by the agency's chief economist about the impact of the disclosure rules.

"I am most troubled that the chief economist's conclusions, and many other comments that the SEC received from the regulated community on the quantitative disclosure requirements, appear to have been completely ignored," McIntosh wrote in a letter to Levitt late last month.
Gramm first said last month that Congress might opt to override the agency's rules on derivatives disclosure. At that time, he criticized the agency's review of the rules' potential impact on firms.
"We haven't dismissed that possibility. We would hope that we can get it resolved without having to resort to that, but that is of course one of the approaches you can go with," a Senate aide said.

But the SEC doesn't have much time to make adjustments, since the lawmakers have only until the end of this month to introduce a resolution under the Congressional Review Act if they want to quickly abolish the SEC's rule.
So far, interviews by the staff of McIntosh's subcommittee with the SEC's chief economist and chief accountant have not been fruitful.
"The initial economic analysis appears to be largely guesswork, and their final economic analysis appears to be based largely on anecdotal conversations," an aide to McIntosh's subcommittee said.

The lawmakers are also troubled that Levitt in a speech last year to the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants seems to have tried to discourage the industry from lobbying Congress about pending accounting rules.
"For Chairman Levitt to implicitly make such threats is an interference of our oversight powers at a minimum, and it's offensive no matter which way you look at it," a Congressional aide said.
